property_summary: For any caller and any msg.value, the reference contract C accepts (does not revert) a fallback call iff msg.value == 10 ether and after a successful call it updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp; the mutant requiring 5 ether will reject 10-ether calls and thus break this rule for some fuzzed amounts (e.g., 10 ether).

For any caller and any block timestamp, if a call to the fallback is made with msg.value == 10 ether the reference contract accepts (does not revert) and updates pastBlockTime to block.timestamp; the mutant that requires 5 ether will reject 10 ether calls, causing the property to fail for some fuzzed msg.value (e.g., 10 ether).

For every call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether, the reference contract only updates pastBlockTime when the supplied block.timestamp is strictly greater than the previous pastBlockTime (so repeated calls in the same block do not change pastBlockTime); the mutant that removed the time check can change pastBlockTime even when timestamp does not advance, violating that invariant for some inputs.

For any caller and any 10 ether call, the original contract never updates pastBlockTime when block.timestamp is not greater than the prior value (i.e., repeated fallback calls within the same block do not change pastBlockTime); the mutant (which removed the time check) can update pastBlockTime even if timestamp didn't advance, so for some inputs the value changes while in the same block.

For every admissible call sequence where fallback is invoked with exactly 10 ether, the reference C only updates pastBlockTime when block.timestamp strictly increases between calls; the mutant (which removed that check) can update pastBlockTime even when timestamp did not increase (e.g., two calls in the same block), so asserting that two consecutive fallback calls in the same block do not change pastBlockTime holds for C but is violated by the mutant.

The contract only updates pastBlockTime when the call's block.timestamp is strictly greater than the previously recorded pastBlockTime; removing that check allows pastBlockTime to be updated even when timestamp does not advance (e.g., two calls within the same block), violating the invariant that two same-block fallback calls leave pastBlockTime unchanged.

Invariant: after any single payable fallback call with exactly 10 ether, the contract's pastBlockTime equals the current block.timestamp (the reference sets pastBlockTime to block.timestamp only when timestamp increased, so if block.timestamp is strictly greater than previous value then pastBlockTime equals the new timestamp; the mutant removes the time check and will set pastBlockTime even when timestamp did not advance, allowing a same-block call to change pastBlockTime and thus violate the relation for some inputs).

After any successful call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and passes the timestamp check, the stored public variable pastBlockTime equals the block.timestamp observed during the call (reference preserves timestamp storage; mutant stores block.number and thus can differ).

For any caller and any timestamp/ether setup where the fallback succeeds, the correct contract stores pastBlockTime equal to the block.timestamp when called; the mutant stores block.number instead and thus for some inputs (where block.timestamp != block.number) the stored public value will differ, violating that invariant.

For any successful payable call to fallback with exactly 10 ether and strictly increasing block.timestamp over the previously recorded pastBlockTime, the reference contract always records pastBlockTime equal to the current block.timestamp; the mutant records block.number instead, so for some inputs (where block.timestamp != block.number) the stored public pastBlockTime will differ and the property is violated.

For any call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and occurs at a strictly later block timestamp than the previous call, the reference contract C only forwards the entire contract balance to the caller when block.number % 15 == 0; the mutant that unconditionally transfers will sometimes drain the contract when block.number % 15 != 0, violating the rule that address(c).balance remains > 0 after such calls at non-drain blocks.

For every call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether from any caller at a strictly increasing timestamp, the reference contract only transfers out its balance when block.number % 15 == 0; the mutant inverts that condition and will sometimes transfer out balance at different block numbers, so the observable address(c).balance after the call can differ between reference and mutant for some block.number values.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether at a strictly increasing timestamp, the reference contract only drains its entire balance to the caller when block.number % 15 == 0 (so address(c).balance == 0 after the call iff block.number % 15 == 0); the mutant inverts that condition and will sometimes drain at block numbers where block.number % 15 != 0, violating this rule.
